title: Latency Claim Audit Cookbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a practical cookbook for auditing and packaging latency claims for the field. It gives a replicable checklist, minimal experiments, the telemetry to pull, math for converting ms wins into dollars, and compact rebuttals vs competitor messaging. Goal: make any latency/cost claim actionable and defensible for sales, partnerships, and legal review.

High-level claim template (for copywriters):
  - Claim headline: We reduce median inference latency by X% (or Y ms) vs. [competitor/model baseline] under realistic customer workloads.
  - Supporting line: Measured on N requests across M customers in production-like environments using sequence distribution S, caching policy C, and batching settings B.
  - Economic translation: X ms → $Z per 1M requests (example math below).

Quick audit checklist (pass/fail + notes):
  1) Claim scope clearly defined (model, sequence distribution, tokens per request).
  2) Baseline defined and pinned (exact competitor model/version or internal v1).
  3) Test surface matches customer behavior (session rates, cold starts, prefix cache warmup).
  4) Test duration >= realistic window (>= 30 min per config, multiple runs).
  5) Environment parity noted (GPU type, batchers, region).
  6) Traffic shape documented (burstiness, concurrent sessions).
  7) Metrics: p50/p95/p99, tail latency count, queued requests, GPU utilization, tokens/sec.
  8) Statistical significance / variance reported.
  9) Safety: not cherry-picked — include worst-case scenarios and fallback behaviors.
 10) Repro script + dataset + random seed + CLI used included.

Evidence matrix (what to include with a claim):
  - Raw timings CSV (timestamp, request_id, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, model, config_tag).
  - Aggregates: p50/p90/p95/p99, mean, stddev by minute.
  - Load profile: RPS over time, concurrent sessions, burst durations.
  - Infra telemetry: GPU/CPU utilization, memory pressure, kernel timeouts, swap events.
  - Cost proxies: tokens served, GPU-hours, pre/post quantization model size.
  - Config diffs: batch size, batching window (ms), KV cache hit rates.
  - Repro README with exact commands and seeds.

Minimum experiment templates (copy-and-run):
  1) Canary microbenchmark (single model, varying sequence length):
     - Run 3 x 30-min jobs at steady RPS for seq lengths {64, 128, 512}.
     - Warmup: 5 min with representative cache traffic.
     - Output: per-minute percentiles + tail counts.

  2) Burst resilience test (simulate realistic spikes):
     - Baseline 50 RPS for 10m, then 1s spike to 1000 RPS for 20s repeated every 5 min, run 60m.
     - Verify p95 and p99 behavior, drop vs queueing, and fallback path latency.

  3) Cost-amortization run (tokens vs latency trade):
     - Run with caching on/off and batching aggressive/moderate.
     - Measure tokens/sec and GPU utilization to compute tokens-per-GPU-hour.

Telemetry snippets (example queries to produce evidence):
  - Per-request export (pseudo-SQL):
    SELECT time_bucket('1 minute', ts) as minute, model, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p50_ms, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95_ms, count(*) as requests FROM inference_requests WHERE test_tag = 'latency-audit' GROUP BY minute, model ORDER BY minute;

  - Tail event counts:
    SELECT model, count(*) FILTER (WHERE latency_ms > 500) as over_500ms FROM inference_requests WHERE test_tag='latency-audit' GROUP BY model;

Conversion math examples (all numbers illustrative — include units when publishing):
  - Example: baseline p95 = 1500 ms, Redwood p95 = 900 ms → improvement = 600 ms per request at p95.
  - If an app has 50M inference requests/month and we focus on p95 tail-improvement that reduces resource overprovisioning: conservatively assume 2% fewer GPU-hours needed. If 1 GPU-hour = $6, monthly spend baseline = $12,000 → 2% savings = $240/mo.
  - Direct per-request amortization (simpler): assume median inference time maps linearly to GPU-seconds consumed per request under continuous load: 
    baseline_avg_latency_s = 1.2s, new_avg_latency_s = 0.9s, savings = 0.3s -> for 50M requests, aggregate saved GPU-seconds = 0.3 * 50M = 15M GPU-seconds = 4166 GPU-hours. At $6/GPU-hour -> $25k/month.
  - Note: above assumes 100% GPU utilization and single-thread mapping; provide conservative / realistic conversion factors per customer (utilization factor, batching, multiplexing).

Packaging guidelines (what to hand to field):
  - One-page PDF: claim headline, 3 bullet proof points, 1 chart (p95 over time), 1 table (config vs numbers), 1 short customer quote (if available).
  - Appendix zip: raw CSVs, SQL queries, scripts, conftest, reproducibility README.
  - Speaker notes: 4 short scripts for common objections (see below).

Sales objection playbook (short rebuttals):
  - Objection: "Benchmarks are synthetic."
    Rebuttal: "We run both synthetic microbenchmarks and customer-like workload tests — the kit we share contains the same sequence distributions and burst profiles many customers see; we also publish reproducible commands."

  - Objection: "This is only for specific GPUs / regions."
    Rebuttal: "We include a matrix of results across T4/A10/GPU-X and provide a routing policy that uses cheaper instances when latency-tolerant; we validate on prem and hosted variants."

  - Objection: "Latency gains won't translate to cost savings."
    Rebuttal: "For many apps the tail drives overprovisioning; reducing p95/p99 reduces required headroom and spikes — we show both direct GPU-hour and operational savings with concrete math and customer case studies."

Competitive quick notes (concise):
  - Competitor A: favors raw throughput, often at cost of tail latency. If quoted against them, emphasize p95 stability and graceful degradation.
  - Competitor B: uses aggressive quantization but with accuracy regressions on long-context tasks. Emphasize our quantization profiles + eval set showing parity.
  - Open-source baseline (LLM v1): easy to match on median under light load, diverges under bursty concurrent sessions — highlight routing + caching advantage.

Redlines and legal guardrails (what marketing must send to Legal):
  - All comparisons must include test dates, model pins, and environment details.
  - Avoid superlatives unless verified across at least 3 independent runs and two hardware families.
  - If customer names or quotes are used, include signed proof.

Risk register (known fragilities):
  - Cherry-picking sequence lengths heavily favors some configurations.
  - Cold-start vs warmed-cache behavior differs; make sure claim language indicates warm/cold context.
  - Quantization interaction with latency: some low-precision formats speed up token generation but change compute mix; validate accuracy.

Quick internal checklist before sending to field: 
  - Evidence zip attached? (Y/N)
  - Repro commands included? (Y/N)
  - Competitor baseline pinned with link? (Y/N)
  - Mathematical conversion conservative assumptions documented? (Y/N)
  - Legal notified and approved? (Y/N)

Next steps (owners and timelines):
  - Run canonical audit on 3 representative workloads (chat small/medium, summarization long-form) — owner: Liam O'Connor — due: 2025-02-10.
  - Prepare one-pager and appendix for field — owner: Asha Kapoor — due: 2025-02-17.
  - Legal review & sign-off — owner: María Torres — due: 2025-02-20.

Appendix: sample reproducibility command lines
  - ./bench/run_inference.sh --model redwood-7b-q4 --rps 200 --seq 128 --duration 1800 --tag latency-audit --warmup 300
  - ./bench/compare.sh --left redwood-7b-q4 --right competitor-x-7b --profile burst-1k --out results.zip

End of document.
